claims.question: q6
claims.claim: Anthropic recommends standing up a quick tool prototype, testing locally, running a comprehensive evaluation, and iterating with agents until strong performance on real-world tasks.
claims.quote: Start by standing up a quick prototype of your tools and testing them locally. Next, run a comprehensive evaluation to measure subsequent changes. Working alongside agents, you can repeat the process of evaluating and improving your tools until your agents achieve strong performance on real-world tasks.

claims.question: q6
claims.claim: Strong evaluation tasks may require multiple tool calls, potentially dozens.
claims.quote: Strong evaluation tasks might require multiple tool calls—potentially dozens.

claims.question: q6
claims.claim: Anthropic used held-out test sets to avoid overfitting to training evaluations, and these revealed additional performance improvements beyond expert-written or Claude-generated tool implementations.
claims.quote: We relied on held-out test sets to ensure we did not overfit to our “training” evaluations. These test sets revealed that we could extract additional performance improvements even beyond what we achieved with "expert" tool implementations—whether those tools were manually written by our researchers or generated by Claude itself.

claims.question: q6
claims.claim: Anthropic reports that resolving arbitrary alphanumeric UUIDs into semantically meaningful language significantly improves Claude’s retrieval precision by reducing hallucinations.
claims.quote: Agents also tend to grapple with natural language names, terms, or identifiers significantly more successfully than they do with cryptic identifiers. We’ve found that merely resolving arbitrary alphanumeric UUIDs to more semantically meaningful and interpretable language (or even a 0-indexed ID scheme) significantly improves Claude’s precision in retrieval tasks by reducing hallucinations.

claims.question: q6
claims.claim: Anthropic warns that too many or overlapping tools can distract agents from efficient strategies, and selective planning of which tools to build can pay off.
claims.quote: Too many tools or overlapping tools can also distract agents from pursuing efficient strategies. Careful, selective planning of the tools you build (or don’t build) can really pay off.
